title: How firms plan to finance AI investment- evidence from the SAFE
gist: ECB SAFE survey of ~5,000 euro area firms shows AI investment plans centre on tools (49%), training (46%) and data infrastructure (40%), but 72% expect to self-fund via internal cash, with bank loans/grants/leasing at 16% each and equity/VC at just 6%. External finance is tied to collateral, so tangible AI capex attracts credit while intangible spend (specialists, training) does not, which the authors warn could slow the scale and pace of euro area AI adoption.

insights.claim: In the ECB's Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) of about 5,000 euro area firms, 49% expect to allocate AI budgets over the next 12 months to AI technologies and tools, the largest category.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Signals broad-based demand for AI software/tools vendors among euro area corporates.
insights.quote: Nearly half of the firms surveyed (49%) expect to allocate their AI budgets to AI technologies and tools
insights.locator: AI is increasingly part of firms' investment plans

insights.claim: 46% of surveyed euro area firms prioritise employee training in their AI investment plans, nearly as many as those buying AI tools, indicating firms see skills as a key bottleneck to AI adoption.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Skills/training spend nearly rivals tech spend, implying adoption is gated by human capital, not only technology.
insights.quote: 46% of businesses are prioritising training for their employees
insights.locator: AI is increasingly part of firms' investment plans

insights.claim: 40% of surveyed euro area firms plan AI-related investment in data infrastructure, while only 12% plan to hire AI specialists and 38% selected none of the AI investment categories.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Low specialist hiring and 38% non-participation suggest AI diffusion in euro area firms is still partial and shallow.
insights.quote: just 12% are targeting the hiring of AI specialists

insights.claim: Larger euro area firms are more likely than SMEs (fewer than 250 employees) to plan AI investment across all categories, though the ranking of investment priorities is consistent across firm sizes.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Points to an AI adoption gap favouring large incumbents over smaller firms.
insights.quote: Larger firms, perhaps unsurprisingly, are more likely than their smaller counterparts to invest across all categories

insights.claim: 72% of euro area firms planning AI investment expect to fund it with internal funds such as cash flow or retained earnings, making internal finance by far the dominant source.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: AI capex in Europe is constrained by corporate cash generation, linking AI adoption pace to profitability cycles.
insights.quote: 72% of firms planning to invest in AI expect to use internal funds such as cash flow or retained earnings
insights.locator: Internal funds are the primary source of financing

insights.claim: Bank loans, grants and leasing are each cited by only 16% of euro area firms planning AI investment, equity and venture capital by 6%, and debt securities by just 1%.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Capital markets and VC play a negligible role in financing euro area corporate AI adoption, a weak spot for European capital markets.
insights.quote: Equity and venture capital are mentioned by 6% of firms, while only 1% are looking into debt securities
insights.locator: Bank loans, grants and leasing play a secondary role

insights.claim: 18% of euro area firms planning AI investment did not select any financing option, suggesting a meaningful segment remains undecided on how to fund AI.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: An undecided cohort represents potential incremental demand for external AI financing products.
insights.quote: 18% did not select any of the financing options listed
insights.locator: Some firms have not yet chosen

insights.claim: Most euro area firms planning AI investment expect to use a single financing instrument, and when they combine sources they typically pair internal funds with external finance; combinations of only external sources are rare.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: External finance acts as a top-up to internal funds rather than a primary driver, limiting leverage-fuelled AI capex.
insights.quote: Combinations involving only external sources are less prevalent.
insights.locator: Most of the firms planning AI investment

themes.theme: Collateral constraint on intangible AI spend

insights.claim: Firms are more likely to use external finance for tangible AI investments such as hardware or data infrastructure because these assets can be pledged as collateral, typically lowering borrowing costs.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Lenders favour tangible AI capex, so hardware and data-centre-type spend is easier to finance than intangible capability building.
insights.quote: Firms are more likely to rely on external finance when investing in tangible assets, such as hardware or data infrastructure.
insights.locator: Collateral affects how firms finance AI adoption

insights.claim: Controlling for country, industry and firm size, planning to invest in AI tools or in data and infrastructure is associated with a 16 percentage point higher probability of combining internal and external financing.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Quantifies the collateral premium: tangible AI investment unlocks external credit materially more.
insights.quote: Both types of investment are associated with a 16 percentage point increase in the probability of doing so
insights.locator: The importance of collateral becomes clear

insights.claim: Hiring AI specialists is associated with only a 9 percentage point increase in the likelihood of combining internal and external finance, and employee training shows no statistically significant effect.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Intangible AI investment (talent, skills) is effectively shut out of bank finance, slowing capability building.
insights.quote: Employee training shows no statistically significant effect.
insights.locator: The picture is different for more intangible spending

insights.claim: Intangible AI investments like specialist hiring and training create value but cannot be used as collateral, making bank financing harder to obtain, while training's small incremental costs are more easily funded from retained earnings.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Bank-centric euro area finance structurally under-serves the intangible side of AI adoption.
insights.quote: external financing for AI investment is closely tied to the availability of collateral
insights.locator: Hardware and data infrastructure often require

themes.theme: Financing frictions may slow euro area AI diffusion

insights.claim: Heavy reliance on internal funds could limit the scale and pace of euro area AI adoption compared with what broader use of external financing could achieve.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Euro area AI-driven productivity gains may lag if adoption stays self-financed, relevant for growth and equity outlooks versus the US.
insights.quote: heavy reliance on this type of funding could limit the scale and pace of AI adoption

insights.claim: The rare use of equity and venture capital for AI investment may point to structural challenges in the euro area financial ecosystem that limit access to financing for intangible investment.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Supports the case for capital markets union-style reforms and opportunities for non-bank lenders/VC in European AI.
insights.quote: That may point to potential structural challenges that limit access to financing for intangible investment.
insights.locator: Bank loans, grants and leasing play

insights.claim: Financing frameworks that support both tangible and intangible AI investment could unlock greater investment potential and accelerate AI diffusion across the euro area economy.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Policy changes targeting intangible-asset financing could be a catalyst for European AI adoption and related lenders.
insights.quote: ensuring that financing frameworks can support both tangible and intangible AI investment could help unlock greater investment potential
